THE WIRE THAT JUMPS — THE MOTION YOU MAKE BY PUSHING CURRENT one bare bar across two rails in a field. push current — F = I·L×B shoves it ALONG the rails and it LAUNCHES.
⚠ I ∥ B → F ≡ 0. The wire goes limp — no leap at all. F lives ONLY where current and field disagree. Turn B back off the bar and the launch returns.

The Rails & the Bar

A single bare copper bar rests across two brass rails in a field pointing into the page (the ⊗ crosses). Current flows in one rail, ALONG the bar, out the other. The field shoves the bar straight down the rails — F = I·L×B — and it launches. Crank the current to launch harder. This is a constant-force kinematics toy, not a circuit sim.

The Launch

force  |F| = B·I·L·cosθ0.00
acceleration  a = F/m0.00
velocity  v = a·t0.00
position  x = ½a·t²0.00

The Current Dial

current I2.8

Bigger current → longer F-arrow, a harder launch. The force is exactly linear in I — double it and the bar gets twice as far in the same time (watch the faint ghost of the last run).

Tilt B Toward the Bar

field tilt θ (B turns toward the current)0°

At 0° the field is into the page (⊗), square to the current: full force. Swing it toward the bar and watch the F-arrow shrink — at 90° the field runs parallel to the current (B ∥ L), the crosses open into arrows, and the bar goes DEAD. The falsifier.

The Switches

Reverse current flips I → the force flips → the bar runs the OTHER way. Reverse field flips B → the SAME flip, a different cause. Launch sends the bar down the rails (constant force while the current flows); it coasts into the end-bumper. There is no spring back — a free bar has no restoring force, the only return is reset.

This is the Whirligig's loop with one side cut free: there two sides make a couple and the loop SPINS; here the lone bar, free to slide, just LAUNCHES — the same F = I·L×B, translation instead of rotation.
